posts.content_md:
With all these different guys out here who have a background in physics, I'm sure that somebody must have tried this. Maybe - maybe not. You never know until you ask around.

It's about an idea I had for making holograms in broad daylight.

It is a well known fact that if you take two polarized sheets of plastic, and place them side by side, you can vary the amount of light that passes through by rotating one of the sheets.

If you rotate one sheet, so that the plane of polarization is at 90 degrees with respect to the other sheet, then no light at all gets through.

Now add a third sheet of polarized plastic.

Rotate the sheet until the plane of polarization is at 45 degrees, with respect to the other two sheets. According to quantum physics, the light now has a 50 - 50 chance of getting through all three of these sheets; although there is no way of telling exactly which particualr photon manages to do this.

But the end result is that 50 percent of your total light manages to pass through . . . . ALL THREE SHEETS OF POLARIZED MATERIAL.

Now to apply this to holography.

Imagine that your holographic plate is protected from ambient, incoherent light, by two sheets of polarized plastic. The sheets are polarized at 90 degrees with respect to each other, and the film doesn't know the difference between broad daylight - at high noon - and a dark room.

None of the incoherent light gets through.

Now imagine that your object beam is polarized at 45 degrees, with respect to both of the sheets of plastic.

Half of the light gets through - so you sacrifice half of your laser light.

But if this works the way I THINK it would, since none of your incoherent light gets through, then it seems possible that you could make a hologram in any light conditions you choose. Of course, you would still have to DEVELOP IT in a dark room, but the level of light present would be unimportant when actually making the hologram.

Of course, the reference beam would have to have the same polarization as the object beam. And while some of the posts on this site talk about horizontal and vertical polarization, and even an "S" polarization with mixtures of both - with horizontal being defined as the best - I really think this is an arbitrary concept.

If you were making holograms on the space shuttle, to give a rather extreme example, the idea of horizontal and vertical would be an arbitrary concept, and meaningless without some kind of reference point.

And I'm thinking that the only reference point that really means anything, on Earth or anywhere else, is the reference beam itself.

So regardless of what actual polarizations you are using, it seems like everything would develop fine on the holographic plate, so long as the object beam and reference beam were aligned properly with each other.

Of course, I could be wrong about all of this, and the only thing that might develop would be an unusual looking H.O.E.

Any ideas?

Yes, must be in between. What's going on is that the linearly polarized light from the first filter is partially passed by the middle (45 degree) filter, but it comes out aligned with the polarization axis of the middle filter and so is partially passed again by the last filter.

The "rope in slot" analogy from this lecture might help you to visualize this:

[http://www.physics.ubc.ca/~mattison/Cou ... /lecture7/](http://www.physics.ubc.ca/~mattison/Courses/Phys309/lectures/lecture7/)

posts.content_md:
Yes, it does ABSOLUTELY have to be in between. No, you don't need Quantum Mechanics. A simple application of Malus' Law is enough. Malus's Law tell us that if light is linearly polarised and it passes through a polarising material whose axis is at some angle theta, then the amplitude of the light passed by the polarising material is given by:

I=I_0*cos^2(theta)

where I is the intensity of the light passed by the polarising material and I_0 is the original intensity of the light . Now, the first polariser, p1, will cause the randomly polarised light to become (say) vertically polarised with say an intensity of 10 W/sq cm. This 10 W/sq cm vertically polarised light hits a polariser at 45 degrees, p2. By Malus Law, the intensity of the light after p2 is 10*cos^2(45) which, since cos(45)=1/sq root(2), is 5 W/sq cm and it's polarised at 45 to the vertical. Now this light hits a third polariser,p3, set horizontally. Since the light after p2 is polarised at 45 and the p3 is set to 0 degrees, the angle between the light's polarisation and the p3's axis is again 45. So, another application of Malus Law gives the light coming out of p3 as 2.5 W/sdq cm (5*cos^2(45)).

I think you seem to confuse polarisation with coherence. It also seems as if you think that somehow incoherent light is mixed in with incoherent light in different states of polarisation. Here's something I wrote on the forum on coherence a while back in this thread: [http://holographyforum.org/phpBB2/viewtopic.php?t=1587](http://holographyforum.org/phpBB2/viewtopic.php?t=1587)

Coherence and polarisation are not intrinsically connected. You can have randomly polarised coherent or incoherent light and also polarised incoherent and coherent light. If you read all the junk below, you might see that outdoor holography is possible since the sun is almost spatially coherent. It subtends an angle of about 1/2 a degree and you need 1/10 of adegree for coherence, so making a small hole in a dark room will give you spatial coherence. Putting a filter in the beam will give you temporal coherence. However, the beam is unpolarised (randomly polarised) and so you still need a polariser.

"We're getting into Coherence Theory here. It's a little difficult to explain without diagrams so this may sound a little convoluted.

There are basically two types of coherence, temporal and spatial. If the source gives out light all of the same color, you have perfect temporal coherence, if not any spatial coherence. You might be able to achieve this by putting a color filter in front of an ordinary light bulb. The better the filter, the smaller the number of frequencies that get through and the greater the temporal coherence, even though the spatial coherence is still almost non-existent. If the source size is small, such as a pinhole, then you have high spatial coherence, if not any temporal coherence. You can achieve this by letting sunlight through a very tiny hole. The sun itself is not very spatially coherent. The angle the sun subtends at your eye is about half a degree, for high spatial coherence, you need to subtend an angle of about 10 minutes of arc (about 1/6 of a degree). If you made a tiny hole through which you allowed sunlight and then put your color filter over this hole, you'd have both spatial and temporal coherence. The degree of spatial and temporal coherence depends on how small the hole is and how few frequencies the filter allowed through. The number of frequencies allowed through by the filter is known as the bandwidth. The laser is a source with an extremely tiny source size and a very small bandwidth and so has a high degree of both temporal and spatial coherence. The coherence length of a source depends on the temporal coherence - the narrower the bandwidth the longer the coherence length.

It's the degree of spatial coherence that determines the wavefront and it's properties. When the source radiates, a source with low spatial coherence will radiate wavetrains from all over it's area at different times. So, if the source is let's say an inch in radius and the source of each wavetrain is 1/1000th of an inch, then the area of the source is 3.141 sq inches and there are 3,141 sources of wavetrains all spurting out wavetrains at different times. It's not really possible to connect the isophase points of wavetrains given out at any time, since a lot of them are given out and emerge at random times. However, if you could narrow down the source size, then only a few wavetrains are given out at any time and now it's possible to select the wavetrains given out in a "spurt" period", follow them and connect points of isophase. A useful analogy may be runners coming out of a room. If the room had large doors so that it could fit many people across it's breadth, then many runners could run out at different intervals and it's difficult to follow a group that came out simultaneously. However, if the door were made smaller and smaller so that fewer people could emerge at any given time, it's possible to track the few that emerged at any time and follow them. If you connected the runners that came out at any given time, the line they made would be the wavefront. If you did the same with birds flying out of a hall, then connecting the birds which the birds flew out of the hall at any time over the area could be connected to give you a 3D "wavefront". You can see that in the case of wide doors (low spatial frequency), the wavefront would be quite complex and constantly changing, while with narrow doors (high spatial frequency), the wavefront is fairly well behaved

Of course, if some people, or birds, ran or flew faster than others, the "wavefront" would quickly distort . That is the line, or area connecting any group of simultaneous "exiters" would distort over time (If some ran faster than others due to different conditions of the medium - say the air was warmer higher up so birds flying higher up go faster - the medium would then be known as "dispersive"). However, if all the runners or birds had the same speed (high temporal frequency) , then the connecting line or area would not distort, but maintain it's shape. If the birds or runners flew or ran - let's stick with the 2D picture so as not to keep repeating "birds or people ran or flew" - if the people who exited simultaneously ran radially outward so they formed an arc of a circle, then this arc would maintain it's shape but expand out ward. In other words, a time lapse photograph would show succesive, expanding arcs. This is a circular - or spherical in 3D - wavefront. In a laser, with it's high spatial and temporal frequency, a wavefront pretty much maintains over very large distances, but not forever to infinity. This is why the slide says "almost". The reason it's not forever to infinity is that even a laser has a bandwidth and a finite source size - it's impossible to have a bandwidth and source size of zero - so you can't exactly track people who came out simultaneously and some people do run faster than others, very, very slightly faster, and so the wavefront will eventually distort. The better the coherence, the longer will the wavefront maintain.

The shape of the wavefront as it's generated depends on the shape of the source that generates it. A very small hole will generate semi-spherical wavefronts. If you block off the outer parts of the semi-spherical wavefront, you have an expanding arc. However, lenses and mirrors function by altering wavefronts. A lens or mirror will take an outward, expanding wavefront and cause it to collapse inward to a point ("focus"). It does this by slowing down different parts of the wavefront by different amounts. if you can precisely slow the more outward ends of a wavefront in exactly a manner that the rate of slow-down depends exactly on how far away from center the wavefront is, you can shape the wavefront pretty much any way you want. The better the lens or mirror, the better this "graduated slow down" of different parts of a wavefront. If the wavefront is not exactly slowed down right, so that a circular wavefront is made into a funny squigly wavefront, you have distortions called "aberrations" by optical types. Hpwever, if you had a perfect mirror or lens, it's also possible to slow down the ends of a wavefront so that the circular wavefront is now flat. This is known as a "plane" wave. "Plane" , because geometrically in 3D space, the semi-sphere has been converted into a flat plane. The advantages of a plane wave is that it not only goes on "forever" (depending of course on spatial and temporal coherence) but it does not fall off as an inverse square of it's distance. Also, when reflected off mirrors, a plane wavefront remains plane . In holography there's another advantage: it's its own conjugate. "

> Might make a different kind of safe light.

It certainly would be different. It's interesting as a thought experiment but doesn't seem practical to me. You'd always have to be checking your source polarizer against the plate because any slight deviation from 90 and you'd get light going to the emulsion.

Is the goal to make a different kind of safe light or to do holography outdoors in the daytime? (Nighttime outdoor holography has been done successfully and is quite fun).

If the latter, it's still not practical because if you're using a low power laser (anything that doesn't pulse with high enough power to get you a latent image in under a micro-second) you'll still need to build a structure around your subject to keep the wind out while you make your multi-second exposure. If you have to go that far, you might as well make the enclosure out of black plastic and put a top on it to keep all the light out.

On the other hand, if you've got a pulse laser, you may as well use an LCD shutter in front of the film that blocks all the light except during the microsecond the exposure is being made.

I'm constantly amazed at the patience you guys have shown with me, and some of my "crazy ideas".

I would like to see holography do everything that conventional photography can do, which includes taking pictures outdoors, in broad daylight.

I think it has just as much potential, at the present moment, as computers had before they really took off. And right now, any amateur - including any single one of us - has the potential to make significant contributions to the field.

For me, that's a part of what makes it so exciting. 

As for pulsed lasers . . . .

I have been looking at the Russian counter-part to Laser Reflections, and they have published some interesting looking schematics. I really don't believe that what they are doing would be that difficult for the amateur, if he or she had the patience to put it together.

While few people might have the money to put together the kind of setup that exists at Laser Refelections, I have been checking out the low power YAG lasers that exist on the market. And I have been pricing some of the other components to. 

While the different parts for this may be more expensive that setups using diode lasers, I think that the average person - with a technical background - could put together a LOW POWER VERSION for about the same price as a home computer.

Just a few thoughts.

Sincerely,

David Potter 8) ( Bird of Prey )

[quote:16d02486ec="Bird of Prey"]I would like to see holography do everything that conventional photography can do, which includes taking pictures outdoors, in broad daylight. [/quote:16d02486ec]

This has been a dream of a lot of holographers over the years. I've been hearing this for over twenty years now!

Most approaches seem to concentrate on the problems of coherence. Unfortunately most books don't do a good job of seperating out temporal coherence from spatial coherence. They just show marching people as opposed to an unruly mob or wave trains in perfect step against waves with different wavelengths - one is "coherent" and the other is "non-coherent" On this theory, most lasers are non-coherent unless you have a bloody good etalon. I've not yet heard a "crazy idea" of outdoor holography centered on the material side of the problem. Is it possible to convert a uniform grey scale image into a set of spatial frequencies? You snap a picture with a conventional camera and either the electronics or the material from which the emulsion is made breaks down the amplitude variations into a frequency variations? I think we're not "crazy" enough! We need to get "crazier"!

By the way, I think it's possible do this conversion with a set of directional FFT's inside the camera.
